title: Indicators of Compromise
summary: An indicator of compromise is a concrete, observable artefact that suggests a system, account or network has already been breached: a file hash, a malicious domain or address, a registry key, a user agent string, an unexpected scheduled task or service, an anomalous account, or a specific line in a log. Such artefacts are collected during incident response and shared as threat intelligence, often in structured machine-readable formats, then matched against telemetry to find other victims of the same campaign or to block known infrastructure. Their strength is speed and precision against threats that are already documented; their weakness is shelf life, because an attacker can recompile a binary, rotate a domain or change a port within hours, and a blocklist built only from file hashes gives a false sense of coverage. The mistakes are hunting indicators without checking the age, confidence and source of the feed, and treating a match as proof of compromise, when shared hosting, stale data and legitimate software produce frequent false positives. An indicator is a lead that requires corroboration, never a verdict.

beginner.definition: An indicator of compromise is a clue that someone has already broken into a system. Examples are a known bad file fingerprint, a strange server address or an unexpected administrator account. Investigators share these clues so other teams can look for the same attacker. The clue tells you what to search for, not the whole story.
beginner.whyItMatters: Once one company is attacked, other companies often face the same tools. Shared clues let you search your own systems before the attacker arrives there. This saves time, because you know exactly what to look for. But clues get old quickly, since attackers change them. So a clue is the start of an investigation, not a finished answer.
howItWorks: An investigator finds something suspicious, such as a strange file or address.
They record it exactly, with the time and the system where it appeared.
They share it with partners, often in a common machine-readable data format.
Your own tools then search your logs and files for the same value.
A match opens a case, where an analyst checks the full context carefully.
The team records which clues were useful and how long each one lasted.
beginner.example: Think of a post office that shares a list of stolen parcel labels. When one of those labels appears, staff know to look more closely at that parcel. The list does not catch every thief, and a label can be reprinted with a new number. So staff still check the sender and the weight, because the label alone is not proof. An indicator of compromise is that shared list for computer systems.
takeaways: An indicator of compromise is a clue about the past, not a live alarm.
Check how old a shared indicator is before you build a blocklist on it.
Combine clues with baseline data, or you will chase harmless matches.

objectives: Explain what an indicator of compromise is and give common concrete examples.
Distinguish indicators of compromise from indicators of attack and behaviour.
Describe how indicators are recorded, shared and matched against telemetry.
Explain why indicators expire and how ageing affects detection quality.
Investigate an indicator match and corroborate it before declaring a breach.
